---
title: "A category-level test of the response scale under the PCM"
subtitle: "Rest-score statistics per category, tested against the CML-conditional table with an exact conditional bootstrap"
author: "Magnus Johansson"
date: today
---

## Purpose

Disordered threshold estimates are often read as evidence that a response
scale is not working as intended. But the partial credit model (PCM) allows
any threshold order, so a disordered estimate is not a misfit to the model.
The question asked here is different: is there evidence that the categories
of an item do not work as the integer scoring 0, 1, ..., m says, whatever the
threshold order? How the middle category is used (for example as "don't
know") is a secondary question.

The approach uses a property of the PCM. Given a person's total score r, the
probability of each category of item i depends only on the item parameters:

$$P(X_i = j \mid r) = \frac{\varepsilon_{ij}\,\gamma^{(i)}_{r-j}}{\gamma_r},$$

where $\varepsilon_{ij}$ is the category parameter and $\gamma_r$ and
$\gamma^{(i)}_{r-j}$ are elementary symmetric functions of all items and of
all items except i. The item-category by score table therefore has expected
counts that involve no person parameters. This is the table behind Glas's CML
test R1c for polytomous items (Glas, 1991). Earlier versions are Glas (1988)
for dichotomous items and Glas and Verhelst (1989) for the MML case.

Two things are added to Glas's table:

- **Statistics per category.** For each category j of the focus item: the
  mean and SD of the rest score among persons in that category, and the
  count of persons in the category whose total score is in the lowest or
  highest 10% of totals, each as observed minus model-expected. Also $Q_j$,
  the sum over score levels of the squared Glas deviates for that category.
  The item index is the sum of $Q_j$ over $j \ge 1$ (category 0 is redundant
  given the others).
- **An exact conditional bootstrap.** Response patterns are sampled from
  $P(\mathbf{x} \mid r)$ given each person's observed total score, so no
  person parameter is drawn. The CML thresholds are refitted in every
  replicate.

Under the PCM, the mean rest score is ordered across categories for any
threshold values, because the item has a monotone likelihood ratio in
$\theta$. So the category means test whether the categories are ordered and
distinct, not whether the thresholds are.

## Design

```{r setup}
suppressMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(tidyr)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(knitr)
})
RES <- "category_conditional_null/results"
s <- readRDS(file.path(RES, "summary.rds"))
alpha <- s$alpha

d <- as.data.frame(s$reps) |>
  mutate(evaluable = is.na(skipped) & !is.na(B_used) & B_used > 0,
         cell = sprintf("n = %d, k = %d", n, k))
ok <- filter(d, evaluable)

cond_labels <- c(
  A0_pcm_ordered    = "PCM, ordered",
  A1_pcm_disordered = "PCM, disordered",
  S_outer_a0        = "Categories 0, 1 interchangeable",
  S_inner_a0        = "Categories 1, 2 interchangeable",
  S_inner_a05       = "Step 2 discrimination .5",
  S_inner_a2        = "Step 2 discrimination 2",
  SWAP_1_2          = "Categories 1, 2 swapped",
  DK_wide_05        = "Don't know 5%, wide middle",
  DK_wide_10        = "Don't know 10%, wide middle",
  DK_wide_25        = "Don't know 25%, wide middle",
  DK_narrow_05      = "Don't know 5%, narrow middle",
  DK_narrow_10      = "Don't know 10%, narrow middle",
  DK_narrow_25      = "Don't know 25%, narrow middle",
  ERS_30            = "Extreme response style 30%")
lab <- function(x) factor(cond_labels[as.character(x)], levels = cond_labels)

# Okabe-Ito, validated for four nominal series (all-pairs CVD dE 11.0).
# The lightest hue goes to the least central series (tail).
pal_stat <- c(Mean = "#0072B2", SD = "#D55E00", Q = "#009E73", Tail = "#56B4E9")
shp_stat <- c(Mean = 16, SD = 17, Q = 15, Tail = 1)
lty_stat <- c(Mean = "solid", SD = "42", Q = "dotdash", Tail = "dotted")
scale_stat <- list(
  scale_colour_manual("Statistic", values = pal_stat),
  scale_shape_manual("Statistic", values = shp_stat),
  scale_linetype_manual("Statistic", values = lty_stat))

stat_long <- ok |>
  select(cond, null, n, k, cell, rep, matches("^p_(mean|sd|tail|Q)_\\d$")) |>
  pivot_longer(matches("^p_"), names_to = c("stat", "category"),
               names_pattern = "p_(mean|sd|tail|Q)_(\\d)", values_to = "p") |>
  mutate(stat = factor(c(mean = "Mean", sd = "SD", tail = "Tail", Q = "Q")[stat],
                       levels = names(pal_stat)),
         category = as.integer(category))
rej <- stat_long |>
  group_by(cond, null, n, k, cell, stat, category) |>
  summarise(rate = mean(p < alpha), reps = n(), .groups = "drop")
```

**Data.** $\theta \sim N(0, 1)$. One focus item (item 1) and $k - 1$ other
items, each with five categories scored 0 to 4 (0 = lowest), so thresholds
t1 to t4 lie between categories 0/1, 1/2, 2/3 and 3/4. The other items follow
the PCM with locations spread evenly over $[-1, 1]$, step pattern
$(-1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5)$ around the location and a fixed jitter (SD 0.2),
the same for every replicate with the same k. The focus item has location 0.
Sample sizes n = 250, 500 and 1000, with k = 5 or 10 items.

**Conditions for the focus item.**

- *Null (PCM holds):* ordered thresholds $(-1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5)$, and
  disordered thresholds $(-1.5, 0.4, -0.4, 1.5)$, in which the middle
  category is rare and never the most probable.
- *Step discriminations* (Glas & Verhelst, 1989, section 7):
  $P(X = j \mid \theta) \propto \exp\{\sum_{l \le j} a_l(\theta - \delta_l)\}$
  with ordered thresholds. $a_1 = 0$ makes categories 0 and 1
  interchangeable, $a_2 = 0$ makes 1 and 2 interchangeable, and $a_2 = 0.5$
  or $2$ makes step 2 flatter or steeper than the scoring assumes.
- *Swapped categories:* data generated under the ordered PCM, then
  categories 1 and 2 relabelled as each other (the second and third
  options).
- *"Don't know" use:* with probability $\pi$ = .05, .10 or .25, the middle
  category is chosen whatever $\theta$. On the ordered (wide middle) or the
  disordered (narrow middle) thresholds.
- *Extreme response style:* 30% of persons answer every item with thresholds
  compressed towards the item location (factor 0.3).

**Tests.** The item index for every item (one-sided), each per-category
statistic for the focus item (two-sided for mean, SD and tail, one-sided for
$Q_j$), all from the same bootstrap. Two comparison tests on the focus item:
a Wald test of threshold order (any adjacent pair with $z < -1.645$, from the
CML covariance matrix, no bootstrap) and a one-sided Wilcoxon test that the
rest score is higher in category j than in j - 1 (the adjacent-category AUC).
The Wilcoxon test has the null that adjacent categories are interchangeable,
so for it a rejection means the categories are distinct.

**Replication.** Null cells 500 datasets with B = 199, alternative cells 200
datasets with B = 99. Monte Carlo SE at a rate of .05 is .010 for null cells
and .015 for alternative cells. Bootstrap replicates in which some category
of some item is empty are dropped, since the CML fit then has fewer
thresholds. A dataset with an empty category in the observed data is
skipped. A dataset in which every bootstrap replicate was dropped is counted
as not evaluable and left out of the rates.

**Run.** Scripts are in `category_conditional_null/R/`. `run_study.R` ran on
10 cores on 2026-11-17 in 2 h 16 min. An earlier run on 2026-11-16 was
discarded because a fixed seed inside the generator for the other items
reset the random number stream, so most replicates in a cell were the same
dataset. `summarise.R` collects the cells and checks that no cell repeats a
dataset. The run computed the elementary symmetric functions by FFT
convolution, which was off by up to 0.001 in the conditional category
probabilities at extreme total scores for k = 10. The scripts now use direct
polynomial multiplication. In 60 datasets (n = 500, k = 10, two conditions)
the change moved the observed $Q_j$ by at most 0.007 and the other category
statistics by at most 0.0001, so the run was not repeated.

```{r evaluable}
d |>
  group_by(cell) |>
  summarise(Datasets = n(),
            Skipped = sum(!is.na(skipped)),
            `No bootstrap kept` = sum(is.na(skipped) & B_used == 0),
            `Kept < 90% of B` = sum(evaluable & B_used / B < .9),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  rename(Cell = cell) |>
  kable(caption = "Datasets per sample size and number of items, all conditions together.")
```

Bootstrap loss is a small-sample problem. At n = 250, about one dataset in
ten kept less than 90% of its bootstrap replicates. The test then conditions
on every category being observed, as it was in the observed data.

## Results

### When the PCM holds

```{r fig-null}
#| fig-height: 7.5
#| fig-cap: "Rejection rate at .05 for each per-category statistic when the PCM holds, by condition, number of items (rows) and sample size (columns). The grey band is .05 plus or minus two Monte Carlo SEs."
rej |>
  filter(null) |>
  mutate(row = paste0(lab(cond), ", k = ", k)) |>
  ggplot(aes(category, rate, colour = stat, shape = stat, linetype = stat)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = .05 - 2 * .0097,
           ymax = .05 + 2 * .0097, fill = "grey85") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = .05, colour = "grey40", linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_grid(row ~ factor(paste("n =", n), levels = paste("n =", c(250, 500, 1000)))) +
  scale_stat +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, .1)) +
  labs(x = "Category of the focus item", y = "Rejection rate") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.text.y = element_text(size = 7))
```

```{r null-index}
ok |>
  filter(null) |>
  group_by(Condition = lab(cond), k, n) |>
  summarise(`Item index` = mean(p_index1 < alpha),
            `Any other item (Holm)` = mean(any_other_holm),
            `Wald, disorder` = mean(disorder_any),
            `Estimates disordered` = mean(disorder_pt),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Rejection rates when the PCM holds. Item index for the focus item, any other item after Holm adjustment over the k - 1 other items, the Wald test of threshold order, and the share of datasets whose point estimates are disordered.")
```

All 20 per-category statistics and the item index reject at between .02 and
.066 per cell, a little under .05 on average. The same holds with disordered
thresholds. The Wald test, by contrast, flags the disordered PCM in 69 to
100% of datasets. So the bootstrap tests treat disorder that the PCM itself
produces as fitting, which is what they are designed to do.

### Detecting a scale that does not work as intended

```{r fig-power}
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Rejection rate at .05 for each per-category statistic at n = 500 and k = 10, by condition. Dotted line at .05. Results for every cell are in the appendix."
rej |>
  filter(!null, n == 500, k == 10) |>
  ggplot(aes(category, rate, colour = stat, shape = stat, linetype = stat)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = .05, colour = "grey40", linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ lab(cond), ncol = 3) +
  scale_stat +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Category of the focus item", y = "Rejection rate") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.text = element_text(size = 7.5))
```

```{r fig-index}
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Rejection rate at .05 of the item index for the focus item and of the Wald test of threshold order, by condition, sample size and number of items. Dotted line at .05."
pal_test <- c("Item index" = "#0072B2", "Wald, disorder" = "#D55E00")
ok |>
  filter(!null) |>
  group_by(cond, n, k) |>
  summarise(`Item index` = mean(p_index1 < alpha),
            `Wald, disorder` = mean(disorder_any), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_longer(c(`Item index`, `Wald, disorder`), names_to = "test",
               values_to = "rate") |>
  mutate(test = paste0(test, ", k = ", k)) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, rate, colour = test, shape = test, linetype = test)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = .05, colour = "grey40", linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ lab(cond), ncol = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual("Test", values = rep(pal_test, each = 2)) +
  scale_shape_manual("Test", values = c(16, 1, 17, 2)) +
  scale_linetype_manual("Test", values = c("solid", "42", "solid", "42")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(250, 500, 1000), trans = "log10",
                     expand = expansion(mult = .12)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Sample size", y = "Rejection rate") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.text = element_text(size = 7.5),
        panel.spacing.x = unit(1.2, "lines"))
```

```{r thresholds}
ok |>
  filter(n == 1000, k == 10) |>
  group_by(Condition = lab(cond)) |>
  summarise(across(t1:t4, mean), `Wald, disorder` = mean(disorder_any)) |>
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Mean CML threshold estimates for the focus item at n = 1000, k = 10, and the rejection rate of the Wald test of threshold order.")
```

The results fall into four groups.

First, **categories that are not distinct or are in the wrong order are
detected, and the thresholds stay ordered.** With categories 1 and 2
swapped, the category means for 1 and 2 reject in every dataset at every
sample size, and the item index in 58 to 100%. The mean threshold estimates
are ordered but close (−0.07 and 0.20 at n = 1000), and the Wald test flags
disorder in at most 0.5% of datasets. With categories 1 and 2 interchangeable, the category 1 mean
rejects in 83 to 100% of datasets and $Q_1$ in 44 to 99%. With categories 0
and 1 interchangeable, $Q_0$ and the category 1 mean carry the signal
(44 to 97%), while the item index is weak (4 to 32%). In these three
conditions the Wald test flags disorder in at most 1.5% of datasets.

Second, **a step that discriminates more or less than the scoring says** is
seen mainly in the category means (23 to 95%). The item index and $Q_j$
are weak here, so a sum of squared deviates is not the best summary for
this departure.

Third, **"don't know" use shows up as a wider spread in the middle
category**, not as a shifted mean. With $\pi$ = .25, the SD of the middle
category rejects in 25 to 92% of datasets (wide middle) and 34 to 98%
(narrow middle), followed by the tail count and $Q_2$. At $\pi$ = .05 the
rates are .05 to .28. On a narrow, disordered middle, "don't know" use at 10%
or 25% removes the disorder: the Wald test flags at most 1% of these
datasets, against 69 to 100% without "don't know" use. Disorder in the middle category
is therefore not a marker of "don't know" use, and "don't know" use can hide
a middle category that is rarely chosen for trait-related reasons.

Fourth, **an extreme response style shared by all items is not detected**
(.01 to .10 for every statistic). The test compares the focus item with the
other items, and a style that affects every item in the same way leaves
that comparison unchanged.

Misfit in the focus item did not lead to other items being flagged. The
Holm-adjusted item index flagged no other item in any alternative cell.

### Adjacent categories: distinct or interchangeable

```{r auc}
ok |>
  filter(cond %in% c("A0_pcm_ordered", "S_inner_a0", "SWAP_1_2")) |>
  group_by(Condition = lab(cond), n, k) |>
  summarise(`0 vs 1` = mean(p_auc01 < alpha), `1 vs 2` = mean(p_auc12 < alpha),
            `2 vs 3` = mean(p_auc23 < alpha), `3 vs 4` = mean(p_auc34 < alpha),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Rejection rate of the one-sided Wilcoxon test that the rest score is higher in the upper of two adjacent categories. A rejection means the two categories are distinct.")
```

The Wilcoxon test separates adjacent categories that differ from those that
do not. When categories 1 and 2 are interchangeable, it rejects for that pair
in 2.5 to 4.5% of datasets, close to its nominal level, while it rejects for
every other pair in most datasets. With categories 1 and 2 swapped it never
rejects for that pair, because the rest score is lower in category 2 than in
category 1. Its null is interchangeability, not the PCM, so a non-rejection
is weak evidence that two categories carry the same information, and a
rejection says only that they differ in the expected direction.

### Using all 20 category statistics together

```{r multiplicity}
pc <- grep("^p_(mean|sd|tail|Q)_\\d$", names(ok), value = TRUE)
ok |>
  filter(null) |>
  mutate(any20 = apply(across(all_of(pc)) < alpha, 1, any)) |>
  group_by(Condition = lab(cond), k, n) |>
  summarise(`Any of 20 at .05` = mean(any20), .groups = "drop") |>
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Share of datasets with at least one of the 20 per-category statistics at p < .05 when the PCM holds.")
```

Each statistic is calibrated on its own, but a reader who looks at all 20
and acts on any p < .05 rejects in 44 to 51% of datasets when the PCM holds.
A Holm adjustment over the 20 cannot reject at all here: the smallest
attainable p is $1/(B + 1)$, .005 with B = 199, and 20 times that is .10. The
item index is the only single calibrated test per item among these
statistics, and it misses some
departures that the category statistics find (categories 0 and 1
interchangeable, step discriminations, "don't know" use).

### Diagnostic plots for single datasets

```{r plot-setup}
source("category_conditional_null/R/calibration_functions.R")
source("category_conditional_null/R/plot_functions.R")
ex <- readRDS(file.path(RES, "plot_examples.rds"))
pv <- readRDS(file.path(RES, "plot_pav_examples.rds"))
ex_conds <- c(A1_pcm_disordered = "PCM, disordered (null)",
              SWAP_1_2 = "Categories 1, 2 swapped",
              S_inner_a0 = "Categories 1, 2 interchangeable",
              S_inner_a2 = "Step 2 discrimination 2",
              DK_narrow_25 = "Don't know 25%, narrow middle")
stack <- function(part) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(ex), function(nm) {
    d <- ex[[nm]][[part]]
    d$cond <- factor(ex_conds[nm], levels = ex_conds)
    d
  }))
}
```

The tests say whether a category departs from the model. A plot can show
how. A bar plot of observed and expected counts per category shows nothing
here: the category counts are the sufficient statistics for the item's CML
parameters, so the expected counts equal the observed counts. Each plot below
therefore splits the persons by total score. The examples are one simulated
dataset per condition at n = 500 and k = 10, generated by
`category_conditional_null/R/plot_examples.R` and `plot_pav_examples.R`.

```{r fig-group-resid}
#| fig-height: 8.5
#| fig-cap: "Standardised residual, (observed − expected) / SD, of the count in each category of the focus item within five score groups of about equal size. Dotted lines at ±1.96. One dataset per condition (rows), n = 500, k = 10."
plot_group_resid(stack("agg"))
```

Swapped categories give a sign reversal across the score range: category 2
is chosen more often than expected in the low score groups and category 1 in
the high groups, with 9 of 25 residuals beyond ±1.96 against 1 of 25 under
the null. Interchangeable categories give a weaker form of the same pattern.

```{r fig-adjacent}
#| fig-height: 8.5
#| fig-cap: "Share of persons in the upper of two adjacent categories of the focus item at each total score, among persons in either category (circles, area proportional to the number of persons), against the CML expectation (line) and its pointwise 95% binomial band (grey). One dataset per condition."
plot_adjacent(stack("adj"))
```

Under the PCM the share in the upper category rises with the total score.
For swapped categories the observed share for categories 2 and 1 falls
across the middle of the score range, and a quarter of the points lie outside
the band. The band is pointwise and treats the item parameters as known.

```{r fig-focused}
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Observed minus expected rest-score mean and SD per category of the focus item (points), against the 2.5 to 97.5% range of the exact conditional bootstrap (grey bars, B = 199). Filled points lie outside the range. One dataset per condition."
plot_focused(stack("boot"), c("mean", "sd"))
```

This plot shows the statistics behind the tests in the earlier sections. In
these datasets the swapped and interchangeable categories shift the means of
categories 1 and 2 in opposite directions, and "don't know" use widens the
middle category.

```{r fig-pav}
#| fig-height: 9.5
#| fig-cap: "PAV-adjusted calibration plots for the cumulative events X ≥ k of the focus item. The forecast is the CML conditional probability P(X ≥ k | r). The line is the conditional event probability from the pool-adjacent-violators algorithm, the grey band the pointwise 95% range of the same curve for responses sampled given the total scores at the fitted item parameters. Dotted diagonal: perfect calibration. One dataset per condition."
plot_pav(pv)
```

The last plot follows the recommendation of Säilynoja et al. (2025) for
ordinal outcomes: one PAV-adjusted calibration plot (Dimitriadis et al.,
2021) per cumulative event. Here the forecast is the CML conditional
probability given the total score, so no person parameter enters, and the
band is drawn from the exact conditional sampler. CML reproduces the
category counts, so the mean deviation from the diagonal is zero for every
event, and only the shape of the curve can depart. A curve flatter than the
diagonal means that the event depends less on the total score than the model
predicts. Swapped and interchangeable categories give a flat curve for X ≥ 2
(62% and 40% of the points outside the band), while the other events stay
close to the diagonal, so the plot points to the step between categories 1
and 2. A step that discriminates more than the
scoring says gives an S-shaped curve for X ≥ 2 (13% outside). None of the
other plots showed that condition. Under the null, 0 to 5% of the points per
event were outside the band.

Pointwise bands are a guide, not a test. Under the null, some point will
often lie outside a band, and in-sample bands of this kind were conservative
in an earlier check of a nine-item PCM (2 to 3% of points outside under the
null, easyRaschBayes `dev/pav-calibration-plan.md`). The next section turns
the PAV curves into a test.

### Null distribution of the residuals in the residual plot

The residual plot above, and `RMitemCatFitPlot(type = "residuals")`, divide
observed minus expected counts by the binomial standard deviation
$\sqrt{\sum_r n_r p_{rj}(1 - p_{rj})}$ over the scores in a group, which
treats the item parameters as known. They are CML estimates from the same
data, and the category counts are their sufficient statistics, so at the
estimates each category's residuals sum to zero over the score groups. That
removes about one of the $G$ degrees of freedom, and the residuals should
vary less than a standard normal, with an SD near $\sqrt{(G - 1)/G}$.

```{r resid-null-load}
rn <- readRDS(file.path(RES, "residual_null_summary.rds"))
rb <- readRDS(file.path(RES, "residual_band_check.rds"))
rpct <- function(x, d = 1) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
rrng <- function(x, d = 1) paste0(rpct(min(x), d), " to ", rpct(max(x), d))
f2 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
c5 <- subset(rn$by_cell, groups == 5)
c3 <- subset(rn$by_cell, groups == 3)
c10 <- subset(rn$by_cell, groups == 10)
b5 <- subset(rn$by_bin, groups == 5)
```

**Design.** PCM data with $\theta \sim N(0, 1)$, $n$ = 200, 500, 1000,
$k$ = 5 or 10 items with 3 or 5 categories (item locations evenly over
$[-1, 1]$, steps evenly over $[-1.5, 1.5]$ with jitter, SD 0.2), and
`r rn$reps` datasets per cell. Residuals were computed as the plot does, from
the CML estimates, and with the generating thresholds, for 3, 5 and 10 score
groups. Datasets with an empty category were skipped (`r sum(rn$skipped)` of
`r 12 * rn$reps`). Script `category_conditional_null/R/residual_null_check.R`.

With the generating thresholds the residuals are close to standard normal
(SD `r f2(min(rn$by_cell$sd_true))` to `r f2(max(rn$by_cell$sd_true))`,
`r rrng(rn$by_cell$beyond_true)` beyond ±1.96), so the binomial variance is
right when the parameters are known. With the estimates, at the default 5
score groups, the SD is `r f2(min(c5$sd_est))` to `r f2(max(c5$sd_est))` and
`r rrng(c5$beyond_est)` of cells fall beyond ±1.96. With 3 groups the share is
`r rrng(c3$beyond_est)` and with 10 groups `r rrng(c10$beyond_est)`. The SDs
are close to what $\sqrt{(G - 1)/G}$ predicts (`r f2(sqrt(2/3))`,
`r f2(sqrt(4/5))` and `r f2(sqrt(9/10))`). Sample size and number of items
make little difference (@tbl-resid-null in the appendix).

The share depends on the expected count in the cell (@fig-resid-null). Cells
with many expected respondents vary least. In sparse cells the residual is
skewed: with 5 groups and fewer than 5 expected respondents,
`r rpct(mean(subset(b5, e_bin == "E < 5")$upper_est))` of cells lie above
+1.96 and `r rpct(mean(subset(b5, e_bin == "E < 5")$lower_est), 2)` below
−1.96. A sparse cell can show more respondents than expected, but almost
never markedly fewer.

```{r fig-resid-null}
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-cap: "Share of standardised residuals beyond ±1.96 when the PCM holds, by number of score groups and expected count in the cell, with the residual computed from the CML estimates (as plotted) and from the generating thresholds. Points: 5 and 10 items. Dotted line at 5%."
fd <- rn$by_bin |>
  select(groups, k, e_bin, beyond_est, beyond_true) |>
  pivot_longer(c(beyond_est, beyond_true), names_to = "par", values_to = "share") |>
  mutate(par = factor(c(beyond_est = "CML estimates",
                        beyond_true = "Generating thresholds")[par],
                      levels = c("CML estimates", "Generating thresholds")),
         e_bin = factor(paste("Expected", sub("E ", "", e_bin)),
                        levels = paste("Expected", c("< 5", "5-20", "> 20"))))
ggplot(fd, aes(groups, share, colour = par, shape = par, linetype = par)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, colour = "grey40", linetype = "dotted") +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "line") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ e_bin) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(3, 5, 10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(100 * x, "%"),
                     limits = c(0, NA)) +
  scale_colour_manual(NULL, values = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00")) +
  scale_shape_manual(NULL, values = c(16, 17)) +
  scale_linetype_manual(NULL, values = c("solid", "42")) +
  labs(x = "Score groups", y = "Beyond ±1.96") +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Fixed lines at ±1.96 therefore flag fewer cells than their nominal 5%, by an
amount that depends on the number of score groups and the cell size, and
they almost never flag a sparse cell for having too few respondents. The
residual plot in the package draws no such lines. When the result of
`RMitemCatFit()` is given as `fit`, each cell instead gets the pointwise 95%
range of its residual in the datasets that function simulated given the
total scores, with the item parameters re-estimated in each. The simulated
datasets share the observed total scores, so the score groups are the same
in all of them. The plot regenerates each dataset from its stored seed and
re-estimated thresholds for the chosen grouping, without refitting.

In `r rb$settings$datasets` PCM datasets ($n$ = `r rb$settings$n`,
$k$ = `r rb$settings$k`, `r rb$settings$m + 1` categories,
`r rb$settings$iterations` simulated datasets each, 5 score groups),
`r rpct(rb$overall$below_range + rb$overall$above_range, 2)` of cells fell
outside their range (`r rpct(rb$overall$below_range, 2)` below,
`r rpct(rb$overall$above_range, 2)` above), against
`r rpct(rb$overall$below_196 + rb$overall$above_196, 2)` beyond ±1.96 in the
same cells. In cells with fewer than 5 expected respondents the range left
`r rpct(rb$by_bin$below_range[1])` below and `r rpct(rb$by_bin$above_range[1])`
above, where ±1.96 left `r rpct(rb$by_bin$below_196[1], 2)` and
`r rpct(rb$by_bin$above_196[1])` (@tbl-resid-band in the appendix). Script
`category_conditional_null/R/residual_band_check.R`.

### Rest-score plot and item discrimination

The rest-score plot shows, per category, the mean and SD of the rest score
of the respondents in that category, observed minus expected given the total
scores. The expected reading for discrimination: if an item discriminates
less than the PCM assumes, its category curves against the total score are
flatter, so each category is chosen over a wider range of total scores. The
rest-score SD within each category is then larger than expected, and the
category means are compressed, low categories above and high categories
below their expectation. An item that discriminates more than assumed should
give the reverse. No condition in the main study varies the discrimination of
a whole item, so this was checked separately.

```{r discr-load}
dr <- readRDS(file.path(RES, "restscore_discr_summary.rds"))
dc <- dr$by_cat
dcell <- dr$by_cell
out_rate <- function(a, n, st, cats) {
  x <- dc[dc$a == a & dc$n == n & dc$statistic == st & dc$category %in% cats, ]
  x$above + x$below
}
```

**Design.** Ten items with five categories, $\theta \sim N(0, 1)$, $n$ = 300
or 1000, `r dr$settings$reps` datasets per cell. The focus item follows a
generalised PCM with slope $a$ = 0.5, 1 or 2,
$P(X = j \mid \theta) \propto \exp\{a(j\theta - \sum_{l \le j} \delta_l)\}$,
with thresholds centred at 0. The other nine items follow the PCM
($a$ = 1). Each dataset was analysed with `RMitemCatFit()` (`r dr$settings$iterations`
simulated datasets) and `RMitemCatFitPlot(type = "restscore", fit = ...)`.
Recorded per category of the focus item: the observed minus expected mean
and SD of the rest score, and whether it fell outside its pointwise 95%
range. Script `category_conditional_null/R/restscore_discrimination_check.R`.

The direction is as expected in every category (@fig-discr). With $a$ = 0.5
the SD is above its expectation in all five categories (by
`r f2(min(dc$mean_diff[dc$a == 0.5 & dc$statistic == "sd"]))` to
`r f2(max(dc$mean_diff[dc$a == 0.5 & dc$statistic == "sd"]))` rest-score
points on average), and the means are compressed: categories 0 and 1 above
expectation, 3 and 4 below, the middle category unchanged. With $a$ = 2 the
SD is below expectation in all categories and the means spread out. With
$a$ = 1 all differences are near zero and each category falls outside its
range in `r rrng(dc$above[dc$a == 1] + dc$below[dc$a == 1])` of datasets.

The SD carries at least as much of the signal as the mean. The mean shifts
most in the extreme categories and not at all in the middle one, while the
SD shifts by a similar amount in every category. At $n$ = 1000 and $a$ = 2,
the middle category's SD fell below its range in
`r rpct(out_rate(2, 1000, "sd", 2), 0)` of datasets, and its mean outside the
range in `r rpct(out_rate(2, 1000, "mean", 2), 0)`. At $n$ = 300 and $a$ = 2,
the SD of the inner categories fell outside in
`r rrng(out_rate(2, 300, "sd", 1:3), 0)` of datasets, the means in
`r rrng(out_rate(2, 300, "mean", 1:3), 0)`.

The two sources of evidence differ in kind, so their rates are not
comparable. The ranges in the rest-score plot are pointwise and uncorrected:
with $a$ = 1, some category of the focus item fell outside its range on the
mean or SD panel in about a fifth to a quarter of datasets. The calibration
test in `RMitemCatFit()` combines the events of an item and corrects across
items, so its rate under the model is controlled. It flagged the focus item
(adjusted $p$ < .05) at $n$ = 300 in
`r rpct(dcell$focus_flagged[dcell$a == 0.5 & dcell$n == 300], 0)` of
datasets with $a$ = 0.5 and `r rpct(dcell$focus_flagged[dcell$a == 2 & dcell$n == 300], 0)`
with $a$ = 2, and at $n$ = 1000 in
`r rpct(dcell$focus_flagged[dcell$a == 0.5 & dcell$n == 1000], 0)` and
`r rpct(dcell$focus_flagged[dcell$a == 2 & dcell$n == 1000], 0)`. So the
calibration test has limited power against a whole-item slope at $n$ = 300,
while the rest-score SD shows the direction clearly. Whether a corrected test
of the rest-score statistics would detect a slope more often than the
calibration test was not examined here. The residual and calibration plots
were not examined in this check.

```{r fig-discr}
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Rest score per category of the focus item, observed minus expected (top) and share of datasets outside the pointwise 95% range (bottom), for the mean and SD panels of the rest-score plot. Focus item slope a = 0.5, 1 (PCM) or 2, n = 1000, 10 items. Results for n = 300 are in the appendix."
fdd <- dc |>
  filter(n == 1000) |>
  mutate(outside = above + below) |>
  select(a, statistic, category, mean_diff, outside) |>
  pivot_longer(c(mean_diff, outside), names_to = "measure", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(measure = factor(c(mean_diff = "Observed minus expected",
                            outside = "Share outside range")[measure],
                          levels = c("Observed minus expected", "Share outside range")),
         statistic = factor(c(mean = "Rest-score mean", sd = "Rest-score SD")[statistic],
                            levels = c("Rest-score mean", "Rest-score SD")),
         a = factor(paste("a =", a), levels = paste("a =", c(0.5, 1, 2))))
ggplot(fdd, aes(category, value, colour = a, shape = a, linetype = a)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey40", linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_grid(measure ~ statistic, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(NULL, values = c("#0072B2", "#000000", "#D55E00")) +
  scale_shape_manual(NULL, values = c(16, 1, 17)) +
  scale_linetype_manual(NULL, values = c("solid", "dotted", "42")) +
  labs(x = "Category of the focus item", y = NULL) +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

### A calibration test from the PAV curves

```{r cal-setup}
cal <- readRDS(file.path(RES, "calibration_summary.rds"))$reps |>
  mutate(evaluable = is.na(skipped) & !is.na(B_used) & B_used > 0,
         cell = sprintf("n = %d, k = %d", n, k))
cal_ok <- filter(cal, evaluable)

# Item p of every item from R/compare_combination.R, which recomputes both
# combinations of the events from the stored bootstrap MCB values:
# p = studentised max-T (used below), p_minp = pooled min-p (the first
# approach), padj / padj_minp = Westfall-Young step-down over the items.
cal_items <- readRDS(file.path(RES, "compare_combination.rds"))$items |>
  transmute(cond, null, n, k, rep, item, p = p_max, padj = padj_max,
            p_minp = p_min, padj_minp = padj_min)
null_cell <- cal_items |>
  filter(null) |>
  group_by(cond, n, k) |>
  summarise(r01 = mean(p < .01), r05 = mean(p < alpha), r10 = mean(p < .10),
            le01 = mean(p <= .01), le05 = mean(p <= alpha),
            min_p = min(p), r05_minp = mean(p_minp < alpha),
            min_p_minp = min(p_minp), .groups = "drop")
null_all <- cal_items |>
  filter(null) |>
  group_by(k) |>
  summarise(r01 = mean(p < .01), r05 = mean(p < alpha),
            r01_minp = mean(p_minp < .01), r05_minp = mean(p_minp < alpha),
            .groups = "drop")
# Family-wise rate: any item of a null dataset with adjusted p below alpha.
fwer <- cal_items |>
  filter(null) |>
  group_by(cond, n, k, rep) |>
  summarise(any_maxT = any(padj < alpha), any_minp = any(padj_minp < alpha),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(cond, n, k) |>
  summarise(datasets = n(), fw = mean(any_maxT), fw_minp = mean(any_minp),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(se = sqrt(.05 * .95 / datasets))
fw_top <- slice_max(fwer, fw, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
# Null check at B = 999, n = 1000 and k = 5 (R/run_calibration_B999.R).
b999 <- readRDS(file.path(RES, "calibration_b999_summary.rds"))$strict
b9 <- function(cnd, col) b999[[col]][b999$cond == cnd]
le_top <- slice_max(null_cell, le01, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
# Focus item after the correction, alternative cells.
pow_adj <- cal_items |>
  filter(!null, item == 1) |>
  group_by(cond, n, k) |>
  summarise(maxT = mean(padj < alpha), minp = mean(padj_minp < alpha),
            .groups = "drop")
pa_rng <- function(cnd, col = "maxT") rng(pow_adj[[col]][pow_adj$cond == cnd])
# Any of the k - 1 other items flagged after the correction, alternative cells.
other_adj <- cal_items |>
  filter(!null) |>
  group_by(cond, n, k, rep) |>
  summarise(any_other = any(padj[item > 1] < alpha), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(cond, n, k) |>
  summarise(rate = mean(any_other), .groups = "drop")
event_null <- cal_ok |>
  filter(null) |>
  group_by(cond, n, k) |>
  summarise(across(all_of(paste0("p_raw_", 1:4)), ~ mean(.x < alpha)), .groups = "drop")
other_alt <- cal_items |>
  filter(!null, item > 1) |>
  group_by(cond, n, k) |>
  summarise(rate = mean(p < alpha), .groups = "drop")

pow <- bind_rows(
  cal_items |> filter(!null, item == 1) |> group_by(cond, n, k) |>
    summarise(rate = mean(p < alpha), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(test = "Calibration test"),
  ok |> filter(!null) |> group_by(cond, n, k) |>
    summarise(rate = mean(p_index1 < alpha), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(test = "Item index"))

# Cells where either test rejects in more than 20%: calibration minus index.
pow_big <- pow |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = test, values_from = rate) |>
  mutate(d = `Calibration test` - `Item index`) |>
  filter(pmax(`Calibration test`, `Item index`) > .2)

# Inline helpers: a rate as a percentage, and a range of rates.
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x)
rng <- function(x) paste(pct(min(x)), "to", pct(max(x)))
f3 <- function(x) sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", x))
pw <- function(cnd, nn, kk, tst = "Calibration test") {
  pct(pow$rate[pow$cond == cnd & pow$n == nn & pow$k == kk & pow$test == tst])
}
pw_rng <- function(cnd, tst = "Calibration test") {
  rng(pow$rate[pow$cond == cnd & pow$test == tst])
}
# Share of the focus item's max-T rejections kept after the step-down across
# items: rate after / rate before, in cells with a rate before above .20.
kept <- pow |>
  filter(test == "Calibration test") |>
  select(cond, n, k, before = rate) |>
  inner_join(pow_adj, by = c("cond", "n", "k")) |>
  filter(before > .2) |>
  mutate(share = maxT / before,
         scale = cond %in% c("SWAP_1_2", "S_outer_a0", "S_inner_a0"))
```

**Statistic.** For item i and the event $X_i \ge k$, the forecast for person
v is $p_v = P(X_i \ge k \mid r_v)$ and the outcome $y_v$ is 1 when the person
scored k or higher. The statistic is the miscalibration component of the
Brier score in the CORP decomposition (Dimitriadis et al., 2021):

$$\text{MCB} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_v (p_v - y_v)^2 - \frac{1}{n}\sum_v (\hat c_v - y_v)^2,$$

where $\hat c_v$ is the PAV-recalibrated probability, the curve in
@fig-pav. MCB is zero when the curve lies on the diagonal and grows with its
distance from it. It is computed for every item and event, without the
persons with an extreme total score.

**p-values.** The reference distribution is the exact conditional bootstrap
used for the category statistics, with the CML thresholds refitted in every
replicate, so the fit of the forecast to the same data is part of it. For
each event, p is the share of the pool of the observed MCB and its B
replicates that lies at or above the observed value. The four events of an
item are combined by a studentised Westfall-Young max-T (Ge et al., 2003). Each event's MCB is centred and scaled by the mean and SD of its pool,
the item statistic is the largest of the four, and the item p is the share
of the pool of item statistics at or above the observed one. This is how the
bootstrap tests in easyRasch2 combine statistics on different scales. Across
the k items, the Westfall-Young step-down on the item statistics gives
adjusted p-values that control the family-wise error rate. A test rejects
when p < .05, as in easyRasch2.

The first version combined the events by a single-step min-p, with Holm's
method across items. Its smallest attainable item p is the number of tied
replicates at the smallest event p divided by B + 1, and with B = 199 no
item p was below .015, so a correction across items could hardly reject.
Both combinations are computed from the same stored bootstrap values
(`R/compare_combination.R`), and the min-p results are reported alongside.

**Run.** Same 84 cells, generators, replications and B as above, with new
datasets. `run_calibration_study.R` ran on 4 cores on 2026-11-18 and 19 in
about 6 h, and `summarise_calibration.R` collects the cells. An earlier run
was discarded. Its min-p step divided the replicates' p by B and the
observed p by B + 1, which left out replicates tied with the observed value,
so the item p was too small (`R/minp_toy_check.R`).

```{r fig-cal-null}
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Share of item p-values (max-T) at or below α when the PCM holds, over all items of every dataset, by condition (rows), sample size (columns) and number of items. Points at α = .01, .025, .05 and .10. Dotted diagonal: a calibrated p-value. The bootstrap has B = 199."
a_grid <- seq(0, .1, by = .0025)
pal_k <- c("k = 5" = "#0072B2", "k = 10" = "#D55E00")
cal_items |>
  filter(null) |>
  group_by(cond, n, k) |>
  reframe(a = a_grid, rate = ecdf(p)(a_grid)) |>
  mutate(k = factor(paste("k =", k), levels = names(pal_k)),
         n = factor(paste("n =", n), levels = paste("n =", c(250, 500, 1000)))) |>
  ggplot(aes(a, rate, colour = k, linetype = k, shape = k)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "grey40", linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_step() +
  geom_point(data = \(d) filter(d, round(a, 4) %in% c(.01, .025, .05, .1)),
             size = 2) +
  facet_grid(lab(cond) ~ n) +
  scale_colour_manual("Items", values = pal_k) +
  scale_linetype_manual("Items", values = c("solid", "42")) +
  scale_shape_manual("Items", values = c(16, 17)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, .05, .1), labels = c("0", ".05", ".10")) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, .05, .1), labels = c("0", ".05", ".10")) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, .1), ylim = c(0, .1)) +
  labs(x = "α", y = "Share of p ≤ α") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

When the PCM holds the item p is close to uniform in its lower tail
(@fig-cal-null). Over all items the rejection rate at .05 is
`r f3(null_all$r05[null_all$k == 5])` at k = 5 and
`r f3(null_all$r05[null_all$k == 10])` at k = 10, between
`r f3(min(null_cell$r05))` and `r f3(max(null_cell$r05))` per cell, and at
.01 between `r f3(min(null_cell$r01))` and `r f3(max(null_cell$r01))` per
cell. The smallest item p is `r f3(min(null_cell$min_p))`, 1/(B + 1).
@fig-cal-null counts p equal to α as well. There the largest shares are in
the `r as.character(lab(le_top$cond))` condition at n = `r le_top$n` and
k = `r le_top$k`, `r f3(le_top$le01)` at .01 and `r f3(le_top$le05)` at .05. The raw p of each event
rejects at a rate between `r f3(min(unlist(event_null[, -(1:3)])))` and
`r f3(max(unlist(event_null[, -(1:3)])))` per cell.

The min-p combination rejected at .05 in
`r f3(null_all$r05_minp[null_all$k == 5])` (k = 5) and
`r f3(null_all$r05_minp[null_all$k == 10])` (k = 10) of items, and never at
.01, since no min-p item p was below `r f3(min(null_cell$min_p_minp))`.

After the step-down across items, the share of null datasets with at least
one item flagged is between `r f3(min(fwer$fw))` and `r f3(max(fwer$fw))`
per cell for max-T. The largest, `r f3(fw_top$fw)`, is in the
`r as.character(lab(fw_top$cond))` condition at n = `r fw_top$n` and
k = `r fw_top$k`,
`r sprintf("%.1f", (fw_top$fw - .05) / fw_top$se[1])` Monte Carlo SEs above
.05 with `r fw_top$datasets` datasets. Every other cell is at or below
`r f3(sort(fwer$fw, decreasing = TRUE)[2])`.

The two null cells at n = 1000 and k = 5 were run again with B = 999 and
`r b999$datasets[1]` new datasets each (`R/run_calibration_B999.R`). The
family-wise rate was `r f3(b9("A0_pcm_ordered", "fwer"))` for the ordered and
`r f3(b9("A1_pcm_disordered", "fwer"))` for the disordered PCM, with a Monte
Carlo SE of `r f3(b999$se[1])`. The item p rejected at .05 in
`r f3(b9("A0_pcm_ordered", "item_05"))` and
`r f3(b9("A1_pcm_disordered", "item_05"))` of items, and at .01 in
`r f3(b9("A0_pcm_ordered", "item_01"))` and
`r f3(b9("A1_pcm_disordered", "item_01"))`. Using only the first 199
replicates of the same datasets gives a family-wise rate of
`r f3(b9("A0_pcm_ordered", "sub199_fwer"))` and
`r f3(b9("A1_pcm_disordered", "sub199_fwer"))`, so B = 199 does not inflate
it, and the `r f3(fw_top$fw)` above is most likely chance in those 500
datasets. This
subsample keeps the mean and SD of the full pool for the studentisation, so
it approximates a run with B = 199. At B = 199 the item p rejects at .01 in
about `r f3(mean(b999$sub199_item_01))` of items, below nominal because of
the coarse grid of attainable p.

In the B = 199 run, the family-wise rate of min-p is between
`r f3(min(fwer$fw_minp))` and `r f3(max(fwer$fw_minp))`, held down by its
smallest attainable p rather than by a correct calibration. Rates per cell
are in the appendix.

```{r fig-cal-power}
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Rejection rate at .05 of the calibration test and of the item index (the sum of the per-category Q statistics, from the first study) for the focus item, by condition, sample size and number of items. The two tests were run on different datasets from the same generators. Dotted line at .05."
pal_test2 <- c("Calibration test" = "#0072B2", "Item index" = "#D55E00")
pow |>
  mutate(test = paste0(test, ", k = ", k)) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, rate, colour = test, shape = test, linetype = test)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = .05, colour = "grey40", linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ lab(cond), ncol = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual("Test", values = rep(pal_test2, each = 2)) +
  scale_shape_manual("Test", values = c(16, 1, 17, 2)) +
  scale_linetype_manual("Test", values = c("solid", "42", "solid", "42")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(250, 500, 1000), trans = "log10",
                     expand = expansion(mult = .12)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Sample size", y = "Rejection rate") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.text = element_text(size = 7.5),
        panel.spacing.x = unit(1.2, "lines"))
```

In every cell where either test rejected in more than 20% of datasets, the
calibration test rejected
`r if (min(pow_big$d) >= 0) "at least as often as the item index" else sprintf("about as often as the item index or more often, at most %.1f percentage points less", -100 * min(pow_big$d))`
(@fig-cal-power). The largest
differences:

- Categories 0 and 1 interchangeable: `r pw_rng("S_outer_a0")` against
  `r pw_rng("S_outer_a0", "Item index")` for the item index.
- Step 2 discrimination 2: `r pw("S_inner_a2", 1000, 10)` against
  `r pw("S_inner_a2", 1000, 10, "Item index")` at n = 1000 and k = 10.
- Categories 1 and 2 interchangeable at k = 10: `r pw("S_inner_a0", 250, 10)`
  against `r pw("S_inner_a0", 250, 10, "Item index")` at n = 250.
- Categories 1 and 2 swapped at n = 250 and k = 10:
  `r pw("SWAP_1_2", 250, 10)` against `r pw("SWAP_1_2", 250, 10, "Item index")`.
- "Don't know" use at 25% on a narrow middle, n = 1000 and k = 10:
  `r pw("DK_narrow_25", 1000, 10)` against
  `r pw("DK_narrow_25", 1000, 10, "Item index")`.

Both tests rarely detect "don't know" use at 5 or 10% (at most
`r pct(max(pow$rate[pow$test == "Calibration test" & grepl("DK_(wide|narrow)_(05|10)", pow$cond)]))`
for the calibration test and
`r pct(max(pow$rate[pow$test == "Item index" & grepl("DK_(wide|narrow)_(05|10)", pow$cond)]))`
for the item index), and the calibration test does not detect the extreme
response style (`r pw_rng("ERS_30")`). For "don't know" use
the SD of the middle category from the first study stays the most sensitive
statistic. Misfit in the focus item raised the rejection rate of the other
items only a little: the median over alternative cells was
`r pct(median(other_alt$rate))` and the largest `r pct(max(other_alt$rate))`
(`r lab(other_alt$cond[which.max(other_alt$rate)])`, n =
`r other_alt$n[which.max(other_alt$rate)]`, k =
`r other_alt$k[which.max(other_alt$rate)]`).

Before the correction across items, the two combinations reject the focus
item about equally often. After the Westfall-Young step-down across the
k items (B = 99 in the alternative cells), the focus item is rejected at
these rates, max-T against min-p:

- Categories 1 and 2 swapped: `r pa_rng("SWAP_1_2")` against
  `r pa_rng("SWAP_1_2", "minp")` for min-p.
- Categories 0 and 1 interchangeable: `r pa_rng("S_outer_a0")` against
  `r pa_rng("S_outer_a0", "minp")`.
- Categories 1 and 2 interchangeable: `r pa_rng("S_inner_a0")` against
  `r pa_rng("S_inner_a0", "minp")`.

Compared with its own rejection rate before the correction, max-T keeps
`r rng(kept$share[kept$scale])` of its rejections for swapped and
interchangeable categories and `r rng(kept$share[!kept$scale])` for the other
departures, in the cells where it rejected in more than 20% of datasets
before the correction. Step 2 discrimination 2 at n = 1000 and k = 10 falls
from `r pw("S_inner_a2", 1000, 10)` to
`r pct(pow_adj$maxT[pow_adj$cond == "S_inner_a2" & pow_adj$n == 1000 & pow_adj$k == 10])`,
and "don't know" use at 25% on a narrow middle at n = 1000 and k = 10 from
`r pw("DK_narrow_25", 1000, 10)` to
`r pct(pow_adj$maxT[pow_adj$cond == "DK_narrow_25" & pow_adj$n == 1000 & pow_adj$k == 10])`.
With max-T, the share of datasets in which at least one of the other items
was flagged after the correction was at most `r pct(max(other_adj$rate))`
per alternative cell, `r pct(mean(other_adj$rate))` on average.

```{r fig-cal-events}
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Rejection rate at .05 of the raw p for each cumulative event of the focus item at n = 1000 and k = 10, by condition. Dotted line at .05."
cal_ok |>
  filter(!null, n == 1000, k == 10) |>
  group_by(cond) |>
  summarise(across(all_of(paste0("p_raw_", 1:4)), ~ mean(.x < alpha)), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(paste0("p_raw_", 1:4)), names_to = "event", names_prefix = "p_raw_",
               values_to = "rate") |>
  mutate(event = paste0("X ≥ ", event)) |>
  ggplot(aes(event, rate, group = 1)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = .05, colour = "grey40", linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_line(colour = "#0072B2") +
  geom_point(colour = "#0072B2", size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ lab(cond), ncol = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Event", y = "Rejection rate") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 7.5))
```

The event that rejects points to the step concerned (@fig-cal-events).
Interchangeable categories 0 and 1 are found through $X \ge 1$, swapped or
interchangeable categories 1 and 2 and a step 2 that discriminates too much
or too little through $X \ge 2$, and "don't know" use in the middle category
through $X \ge 2$ and $X \ge 3$. Rates per cell for the item p and each event
are in the appendix.

### Misfit that is not about the categories

A flag from `RMitemCatFit()` is meant to say that the categories of an item
do not work as scored. An item can also misfit the PCM while its categories
work as scored, and the rest-score check above showed that a whole-item
slope moves the category statistics. This run asks how often
`RMitemCatFit()` flags such items, and whether conditional infit separates
the two kinds of misfit.

```{r spec-load}
sp <- readRDS(file.path(RES, "specificity_summary.rds"))
sr <- sp$rates
sf <- sp$focus_items
spec_labels <- c(cond_labels,
  U_multi_r75 = "Second dimension, r = .75",
  U_slope_055 = "Slope 0.55",
  O_ld_d1     = "Response dependence, d = 1",
  O_slope_16  = "Slope 1.6")
slab <- function(x) factor(spec_labels[as.character(x)], levels = spec_labels)
nuis <- c("U_multi_r75", "U_slope_055", "O_ld_d1", "O_slope_16")
sv <- function(col, cnd) sr[[col]][sr$cond %in% cnd]
# Focus-item flags by RMitemCatFit() without an infit flag, as a share of all
# its flags, pooled over cells.
cat_alone <- function(cnd) {
  d <- sf[sf$cond %in% cnd, ]
  sum(d$cat_flag & !d$inf_flag) / sum(d$cat_flag)
}
cat_alone_n <- function(cnd) {
  d <- sf[sf$cond %in% cnd, ]
  c(alone = sum(d$cat_flag & !d$inf_flag), flags = sum(d$cat_flag),
    datasets = nrow(d))
}
# Agreement with the main run, which used other datasets: focus item after
# the step-down, the 14 shared conditions at n = 250 and 500.
spec_vs_main <- cal_items |>
  filter(!null, item == 1, n %in% c(250, 500)) |>
  group_by(cond, n, k) |>
  summarise(main = mean(padj < alpha), .groups = "drop") |>
  inner_join(select(sr, cond, n, k, catfit), by = c("cond", "n", "k")) |>
  mutate(diff = catfit - main)
# Among datasets with the focus item flagged by RMitemCatFit(): share with
# one event, and with two or more, at uncorrected p < .05.
ev_share <- function(cnd, one = TRUE) {
  d <- sf[sf$cond %in% cnd & sf$cat_flag, ]
  if (one) mean(d$events == 1) else mean(d$events >= 2)
}
cat_conds <- c("SWAP_1_2", "S_outer_a0", "S_inner_a0", "S_inner_a2")
spec_used <- sum(sp$skipped$used)
spec_reps <- sum(sp$skipped$reps)
```

**Design.** The design of the main study at $n$ = 250 and 500 and $k$ = 5
and 10, with all its conditions and four more. In the four, the categories
of the focus item work as scored and the item misfits in another way:

- **Second dimension.** The focus item follows the PCM in $\theta_2$, which
  correlates .75 with $\theta$.
- **Low slope.** Generalised PCM with slope 0.55.
- **Response dependence.** The location of the focus item is shifted by
  $d\,z$ with $d$ = 1 and $z = (2x_p - m)/m$, where $x_p$ is the response to
  the other item nearest location 0, as in the Q3 study.
- **High slope.** Generalised PCM with slope 1.6.

The levels were set so that the focus item's conditional infit matches the
misfit of real items in the phq9 data, about 1.28 for underfit and 0.83 for
overfit (script `category_conditional_null/R/infit_calibration_stylised.R`).
Each direction has one mechanism and one slope with similar infit. Mean
infit of the focus item in this run was
`r f2(min(sv("mean_infit", nuis[1:2])))` to
`r f2(max(sv("mean_infit", nuis[1:2])))` in the underfit conditions and
`r f2(min(sv("mean_infit", nuis[3:4])))` to
`r f2(max(sv("mean_infit", nuis[3:4])))` in the overfit conditions.

Every dataset got both tests:

- **`RMitemCatFit()`.** The calibration test of the previous section, with
  max-T over the events and the Westfall-Young step-down across items.
- **Conditional infit** from `RMitemInfit()`. The p-values come from one
  reference set per $n$, $k$ and focus-item thresholds: 1000 datasets
  simulated from the PCM at the generating parameters. Each item's infit is
  studentised by the mean and SD of the observed and reference values
  together and tested two-sided, with the Westfall-Young step-down across
  items. `RMitemInfit()` itself simulates at the estimated parameters, so
  its rates can differ from those here.

PCM cells have 500 datasets ($B$ = 199) and the others 200 ($B$ = 99).
`r format(spec_used, big.mark = ",")` of `r format(spec_reps, big.mark = ",")`
datasets were used. The others had an empty category. An item counts as
flagged when its adjusted $p$ is below .05. Scripts
`category_conditional_null/R/specificity_functions.R`,
`run_specificity_study.R` and `summarise_specificity.R`.

The rates of `RMitemCatFit()` for the conditions shared with the main run
agree with it within simulation error. The largest difference in the focus
item's rate was `r round(100 * max(abs(spec_vs_main$diff)))` percentage
points, over `r nrow(spec_vs_main)` cells with 200 datasets each.

**When the PCM holds.** Both tests keep their rates. The focus item was
flagged by infit in `r rrng(sv("infit", c("A0_pcm_ordered", "A1_pcm_disordered")))`
of datasets and by `RMitemCatFit()` in
`r rrng(sv("catfit", c("A0_pcm_ordered", "A1_pcm_disordered")))`. Some other
item was flagged in `r rrng(sv("infit_any_other", c("A0_pcm_ordered", "A1_pcm_disordered")))`
(infit) and `r rrng(sv("catfit_any_other", c("A0_pcm_ordered", "A1_pcm_disordered")))`
(`RMitemCatFit()`) of datasets.

**Misfit that is not about the categories** (@fig-spec).
`RMitemCatFit()` rarely flagged an overfitting item:
`r rrng(sv("catfit", "O_ld_d1"))` of datasets under response dependence and
`r rrng(sv("catfit", "O_slope_16"))` under slope 1.6, against
`r rrng(sv("infit", "O_ld_d1"))` and `r rrng(sv("infit", "O_slope_16"))` for
infit. It flagged an underfitting item more often, in
`r rrng(sv("catfit", "U_multi_r75"))` of datasets with a second dimension and
`r rrng(sv("catfit", "U_slope_055"))` with slope 0.55, rising with $n$ and
$k$. Infit flagged the same items in `r rrng(sv("infit", "U_multi_r75"))`
and `r rrng(sv("infit", "U_slope_055"))`. In the four conditions together,
`RMitemCatFit()` flagged the focus item in
`r cat_alone_n(nuis)[["flags"]]` of `r format(cat_alone_n(nuis)[["datasets"]], big.mark = ",")`
datasets, and in `r cat_alone_n(nuis)[["alone"]]` of these infit did not flag
it.

**Category problems also show in infit.** Most of the category conditions
make the focus item underfit. Infit flagged it in
`r rrng(sv("infit", "SWAP_1_2"))` of datasets with swapped categories, in
`r rrng(sv("infit", "S_inner_a0"))` with categories 1 and 2 interchangeable
and in `r rrng(sv("infit", "S_outer_a0"))` with categories 0 and 1
interchangeable. Unlike the misfit conditions, these give many flags from
`RMitemCatFit()` alone. Without an infit flag were
`r rpct(cat_alone("SWAP_1_2"), 0)` of its flags with swapped categories,
`r rpct(cat_alone("S_outer_a0"), 0)` with categories 0 and 1
interchangeable and `r rpct(cat_alone("S_inner_a0"), 0)` with categories 1
and 2 interchangeable. For swapped categories and for categories 1 and 2
interchangeable the share fell as $n$ and $k$ grew and infit caught up.

Under the extreme response style, every item departs, and infit flagged some
other item in `r rrng(sv("infit_any_other", "ERS_30"))` of datasets.
Under response dependence the partner item departs too, and infit flagged
some other item in
`r rrng(sv("infit_any_other", "O_ld_d1"))`. `RMitemCatFit()` flagged some
other item in `r rrng(sv("catfit_any_other", nuis))` of datasets across the
four misfit conditions. Rates for every cell are in the appendix.

**Reading a flag.** Two readings follow from these rates:

- **A flag on an item that fits by infit points to the categories.** The
  four misfit conditions almost never produced this pattern, and the
  category conditions often did.
- **A flag on an underfitting item does not by itself say what is wrong.**
  A low slope or a second dimension can produce it, and so can a category
  problem. Swapped categories produced both flags in
  `r rrng(sv("both", "SWAP_1_2"))` of datasets, so setting such flags aside
  as an item problem would miss most swaps. The number of events that
  depart helps. Among flagged datasets, the item with slope 0.55 departed
  (uncorrected $p$ < .05) in two or more events in
  `r rpct(ev_share("U_slope_055", FALSE), 0)` and the item with a second
  dimension in `r rpct(ev_share("U_multi_r75", FALSE), 0)`, mostly in
  $X \ge 2$ and $X \ge 3$. Swapped or interchangeable categories and a
  step with a different discrimination departed in a single event in
  `r rrng(sapply(cat_conds, ev_share), 0)`. In the rest-score plot a low
  slope also raises the SD in every category (@fig-discr).

An overfitting item with a flag did not occur often enough here to say much
about it.

```{r fig-spec}
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Focus item flagged (adjusted p < .05) by RMitemCatFit() only, by both tests, or by conditional infit only, per condition and cell. Top: the categories do not work as scored. Bottom: the categories work as scored and the item misfits in another way. Rates for every cell are in the appendix."
spec_fig <- sr |>
  filter(!null) |>
  mutate(Condition = slab(cond),
         group = factor(ifelse(cond %in% nuis, "Other misfit", "Categories"),
                        levels = c("Categories", "Other misfit")),
         cell = factor(sprintf("n = %d, k = %d", n, k),
                       levels = sprintf("n = %d, k = %d", rep(c(250, 500), 2),
                                        rep(c(5, 10), each = 2)))) |>
  select(Condition, group, cell, `RMitemCatFit() only` = catfit_only,
         Both = both, `Infit only` = infit_only) |>
  pivot_longer(c(`RMitemCatFit() only`, Both, `Infit only`),
               names_to = "pattern", values_to = "rate") |>
  mutate(pattern = factor(pattern, levels = c("RMitemCatFit() only", "Both",
                                              "Infit only")),
         Condition = factor(Condition, levels = rev(levels(Condition))))
ggplot(spec_fig, aes(rate, Condition, colour = pattern, shape = pattern)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_grid(group ~ cell, scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(NULL, values = c("#0072B2", "#000000", "#D55E00")) +
  scale_shape_manual(NULL, values = c(16, 15, 2)) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), breaks = c(0, .5, 1),
                     labels = c("0", ".5", "1")) +
  labs(x = "Share of datasets", y = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.text = element_text(size = 8),
        panel.spacing.x = unit(0.8, "lines"))
```

## Discussion

The category-level statistics detect response scales that do not work as
the scoring says in cases where the thresholds are ordered (swapped or
interchangeable categories), and they do not flag disordered thresholds
when the PCM holds. In these data, disordered threshold estimates were
neither necessary nor sufficient for a response scale that does not work.
Swapped and interchangeable categories gave ordered estimates, the PCM with
disordered thresholds fits, and "don't know" use removed a disorder that was
there.

The calibration test gives one calibrated p per item that finds most of
what the 20 category statistics find, including the departures the item
index misses. It also says which step is affected. The category statistics
remain useful for describing a departure once it is found, in particular the
SD of the middle category for "don't know" use.

A flag is not specific to the categories. An underfitting item with
categories that work as scored was flagged in up to a third of datasets in
these cells, and the category problems often made the item underfit as well.
What separates the two is infit together with the flag. A flag on an item
that fits by infit pointed to the categories. On an underfitting item, the
number of events that depart separated the two in most datasets: two or
more, mostly the middle ones, for a low slope or a second dimension, and
one for a category problem. This is a tendency and not a rule, and a single
dataset can show either pattern for either cause.

Limitations of this run:

- **Multiplicity.** The study has no calibrated decision rule across the 20
  statistics. A joint test needs the bootstrap distribution of all
  statistics together (for example a min-p or max-T adjustment, as in
  Westfall-Young), which this run did not save, and a larger B. For the
  calibration test the max-T step-down across items held the family-wise
  rate near .05, which a run with B = 999 at n = 1000 and k = 5 confirmed.
  Other sample sizes and k = 10 were checked at B = 199 only.
- **One focus item.** Only item 1 departs from the PCM, and it is located at
  the centre of the person distribution. Departures in several items at once,
  and in items off target, are not studied.
- **Bootstrap loss at n = 250.** About one dataset in ten lost more than 10%
  of its bootstrap replicates, and eight datasets lost all of them.
- **Person-level mechanisms.** A response style shared by all items is out
  of reach of a test that compares items. A mixture Rasch model or an IRTree
  model would be needed for that.
- **Mechanisms are stylised.** "Don't know" use is modelled as a fixed
  probability of choosing the middle category, unrelated to $\theta$.
- **Other misfit at one level each.** The specificity run has one level of
  each of four mechanisms, at $n \le 500$. Larger samples, smaller or larger
  departures, and items misfitting in more than one way were not studied.
- **Infit reference at the generating parameters.** The infit p-values in
  the specificity run come from datasets simulated at the true parameters,
  not from the parametric bootstrap at the estimates that `RMitemInfit()`
  uses.

```{r appendix-spec-other}
            `Other item, infit` = rpct(infit_any_other, 1),

            `Mean infit` = f2(mean_infit)) |>
  kable(align = "llrrrr", row.names = FALSE,
        caption = "Specificity run: datasets used, share of datasets with some other item flagged by conditional infit and by RMitemCatFit(), and the focus item's mean infit, per condition and cell.")
```
